value.overview: The Roadside Hawk (Rupornis magnirostris) is a small, widespread bird of prey found from Mexico through Central America and across much of South America. It is named for its habit of perching beside roads and other clearings while hunting. Adaptable and vocal, it uses forest edges, farmland, river margins, open woodland, and some urban areas. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar resident hawk and is often easy to observe from roadsides and rural settlements.
value.classification: The Roadside Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the order Accipitriformes. It is the only species currently placed in the genus Rupornis.
value.identification: This relatively small hawk has a compact body, broad wings, and a long, banded tail. Adults commonly show a gray head and upperparts, finely barred underparts, and noticeable rufous coloring on the wings and belly, although plumage varies among subspecies. The strongly hooked bill and yellow cere, legs, and feet are typical. Its sharp, repeated calls are often heard before the bird is located. It frequently sits upright on exposed branches, poles, fences, or roadside wires.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and across much of South America east of the Andes. In Costa Rica, the Roadside Hawk is a widespread and commonly observed resident, occurring in both the Caribbean and Pacific regions, including lowlands, foothills, valleys, and some settled areas. It favors forest edges, secondary woodland, riparian vegetation, plantations, pasture with trees, agricultural landscapes, and roadsides. It generally avoids extensive unbroken rainforest and very open habitats lacking perches.
value.migrationStatus: The Roadside Hawk is generally nonmigratory in Costa Rica and is considered a year-round resident there. Some northern populations farther north in the range may move seasonally, but Costa Rican birds do not normally undertake long-distance migration.
value.breeding: Roadside Hawks build large stick nests, usually high in a tree and sometimes concealed among vines. Nests may be placed in forest edges, riparian woodland, farmland, or other habitats with scattered mature trees. Both adults help construct the nest and may line it with fresh green leaves. The usual clutch contains one or two eggs. Incubation lasts about 33–37 days, and young typically remain in the nest for roughly 38 days after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: This hawk is an opportunistic predator whose diet varies with location and season. It takes large insects, amphibians, lizards, snakes, small mammals, and small birds. It usually hunts from a conspicuous perch, dropping quickly to the ground or vegetation to capture prey. Roadside Hawks may also exploit army-ant swarms, grass fires, or other disturbances that flush insects and small animals into the open.
value.behavior: Roadside Hawks are conspicuous, vocal birds that often perch beside roads, trails, fields, and clearings. Their flight commonly consists of several rapid wingbeats followed by short glides, and they may wag the tail after landing. Pairs become especially noisy and active around nest sites, where they may circle together and defend the surrounding area. Their tolerance of modified habitats helps explain why they are frequently encountered in Costa Rican agricultural and suburban landscapes.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered increasing.
